title: The Nazareth sermon (Luke 4:16–30)
hook: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, freedom to captives

segments.voice: Yesterday, adam: Luke's family tree ran back past Abraham to Adam, son of God. Your line was everyone's family.

After the desert, Jesus comes back to Galilee, and word about him spreads. Then he goes home to Nazareth, where he was brought up. On the Sabbath he goes into the synagogue, as was his custom. These people watched him grow up and know his family. He stands up to read, the attendant hands him the scroll of the prophet Isaias, and he unrolls it and finds the place he's looking for.
screen: `HOME TO NAZARETH.` → `AS WAS HIS CUSTOM.` → `THE SCROLL OF ISAIAS.`

segments.voice: He reads, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Wherefore he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." And on: to heal the contrite of heart, to preach deliverance to the captives and sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord. Anointed is the root of the title Christ: Christos, the anointed one, in Hebrew Messiah. The acceptable year echoes the jubilee in the law of Moses, when land went back to its families and those sold into service went free. Then he rolls up the scroll and sits down, the posture of a teacher. Every eye is on him. And the sermon Luke gives us is one sentence: "This day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears." At first they marvel at his gracious words. Then someone says: isn't this Joseph's son? Jesus answers that no prophet is accepted in his own country, and reminds them of two old stories we read a few weeks ago: Elias was sent not to the widows of Israel but to a widow in Sarepta of Sidon; Eliseus healed not the lepers of Israel but Naaman the Syrian. God's blessing, going to outsiders. The hometown crowd is filled with anger, and they drive him to the brow of the hill to throw him down. But he, passing through the midst of them, went his way. Luke puts this near the start of the ministry, and some readers hear it as a program for all that follows: good news for the poor, and a welcome wider than anyone expected.
screen: `THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD IS UPON ME.` · `ANOINTED: CHRISTOS, MESSIAH.` · `THE ACCEPTABLE YEAR: A JUBILEE.` · `ISN'T THIS JOSEPH'S SON?` · then, large: `THIS DAY IS FULFILLED THIS SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: Find Luke 4:18 and read it aloud, slowly, the way Jesus did in the synagogue, or just say the phrases: good news to the poor, healing for the brokenhearted, deliverance to captives, sight to the blind, liberty for the bruised. Let each phrase land on a real person you know: someone poor, someone heartbroken, someone stuck. If you pray, hold each of them before God.
Christos. Greek for the anointed one: the title's root, read aloud by Jesus in the Nazareth synagogue the day he said this scripture is fulfilled. Today's word.
Your line: good news to the poor. The first words of his work, read aloud at home. Day four hundred fifty-one, done.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke 4:16–21 at the Chrism Mass of Holy Week, when the bishop blesses the holy oils, and on a Sunday in Ordinary Time in the year of Luke's Gospel.

fork.setup: you're in the Nazareth synagogue. the carpenter's son has just read Isaiah, said it's fulfilled today, and reminded you that God once blessed a foreign widow and a Syrian general. what does the crowd do?
options: ask him for the miracles he did in other towns, and wait politely.
fill with anger and drive him to the brow of the hill.
fork.reveal: they're filled with anger and try to throw him down. but he, passing through the midst of them, went his way.

original.note: Greek: he has anointed me, Luke 4:18; from chrio, to anoint, the root of Christos, the anointed one.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus read a nice verse in church.
what it means: in his own hometown, Jesus announces his mission from Isaiah, good news for the poor, and is nearly killed for saying God's welcome reaches outsiders.
what a scholar hears: the reading combines Isaiah 61:1–2 with a line from 58:6; the acceptable year recalls the jubilee of Leviticus 25; Luke places it as a programmatic opening.

chat.says: What happened when Jesus preached in his hometown, Nazareth?
options: He read Isaiah, said today it's fulfilled, and the hometown crowd turned on him.
He healed every sick person in town, and they made him their teacher.
He read from the law of Moses, and they asked him to stay and teach.
chat.meaning: At Nazareth he read Isaiah, the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, and said this day is fulfilled. When he spoke of outsiders, they drove him out.

jubilee.meaning: in the law of Moses, a year of release

Sarepta.meaning: the town of the widow Elias was sent to

Eliseus.meaning: the Douay's name for the prophet Elisha

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the invented "bought tables from his father"; corrected the jubilee (Leviticus 25 returns land and frees those sold into service; debt release is the sabbatical year of Deuteronomy 15); "his sermon is one sentence" now "the sermon Luke gives us"; "programmatic" reading attributed to some readers; myth 1 reworded; cut the unsourced "often quoted in social teaching".
Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 4:18 and 4:21 quoted from memory; please check. The rest of 4:18–19 is paraphrased, close to the Douay.
The Douay's 4:19 adds 'and the day of reward' (from the Vulgate); the script doesn't raise the common claim that Jesus stopped before 'the day of vengeance'.
The writer's illustration about buying tables from Joseph was cut in the 2026-10-01 review as invention.
The widow of Sarepta and Naaman were days 409 and 413 ('a few weeks ago'). Confirm phrasing.
Luke 4:16–21 at the Chrism Mass and on the 3rd Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year C: confirm.
The Nazareth crowd is described as 'the hometown crowd'; the script avoids framing it as Jews against Jesus.
